question: In which fiscal year's 10-K did NVIDIA first mention the EU AI Act in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
**NVIDIA first named the EU AI Act in its FY2024 10-K** (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024), in Item 1A (Risk Factors):

> "Furthermore, the EU AI Act could impose onerous obligations that may disproportionately impact and disadvantage us and require us to change our business practices." [1], [9]

Context across the indexed years (FY2022–FY2026):

| Fiscal year | EU AI Act mention |
|---|---|
| FY2022 | None [16] |
| FY2023 | No named mention, but referenced "a proposed European regulation related to AI that, if adopted, could impose onerous obligations…" [11] |
| **FY2024** | **First named "EU AI Act"** — new this year [1], [9] |
| FY2025 | Expanded: notes the Act "became effective on August 1, 2024 and will be fully applicable after a two-year transitional period" [2], [3], [8] |
| FY2026 | Carried forward substantially unchanged [4], [5], [6] |

Note: in FY2024 the disclosure was a forward-looking, pre-effective-date risk statement; the "became effective August 1, 2024" language first appears in FY2025.

question: In which fiscal year's 10-K did AMD first mention ZT Systems in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer: AMD first mentioned **ZT Systems in its fiscal year 2024 10-K** (year ended December 28, 2024), with no mentions in FY2021–FY2023. It appeared in both **Item 1A (Risk Factors)**—discussing closing conditions and a potential $300 million termination fee [2][12]—and **Item 7 (MD&A)**, describing the August 2024 agreement to acquire ZT Systems [4][6].

question: NVIDIA used to discuss the terminated Arm acquisition in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7). Which fiscal year's filing was the last to mention it?
answer:
**Fiscal year 2024** (10-K for the year ended Jan 28, 2024) is the last NVIDIA filing whose Item 1A/Item 7 text discusses the terminated Arm acquisition.

- **FY2024 (last mention, MD&A):** "Fiscal year 2023 also included a $1.4 billion acquisition termination charge related to the proposed Arm transaction" [24], and a dedicated "Acquisition Termination Cost" paragraph: "We recorded an acquisition termination cost related to the Arm transaction of $1.4 billion in fiscal year 2023 reflecting the write-off of the prepayment provided at signing" [25].
- **FY2023:** full narrative still present in both sections — "In February 2022, NVIDIA and SoftBank announced the termination of the Share Purchase Agreement... due to significant regulatory challenges" [3], plus the risk-factor discussion of regulatory approval risk citing Arm [5].
- **FY2025:** the narrative detail drops out of risk factors/MD&A; the charge appears only in the segment reconciliation table ("Acquisition termination cost — — (1,353)") and in Note 2, i.e., the financial statements [16][2], not Item 1A or Item 7 [17][18].
- **FY2026:** no Arm-termination disclosure found in Item 1A or Item 7 (the acquisition risk factor is now generic) [22][21].

Note: the Arm termination is still footnoted in Item 15/Note 2 in FY2025 [2]; the claim history confirms the Item 1A/MD&A claims were "dropped" after FY2024 (data covers FY2022–FY2026) [13][14].

question: Is COVID-19 still mentioned in the risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7) in Qualcomm's latest 10-K? If not, when did it last appear?
answer:
**No — COVID-19 is not mentioned by name in Qualcomm's FY2025 10-K (fiscal year ended September 28, 2025), in either Item 1A or Item 7.**

**What the FY2025 filing says instead** — the pandemic risk has been folded into generic "pandemic/health crisis" language:
- Item 1A: risk factors refer to "pandemics or other health crises affecting any of the regions in which we operate" as a disruption to demand, supply, foundries and workforce [6], and to "health crises, including epidemics or pandemics, and government and business responses thereto" affecting manufacturing facilities via quarantines or closures [8].
- Item 7: no reference to COVID-19 or pandemics at all; the forward-looking outlook covers U.S./China trade relations and legal proceedings [10].

**When it last appeared: the FY2023 10-K (fiscal year ended September 24, 2023), in Item 1A only** — COVID-19 was still named in four places:
- "pandemics such as the COVID-19 pandemic" in the geopolitical-conflict/natural-disaster risk factor [11]
- the workforce-practices discussion, noting the pandemic caused modified work practices and a subsequent return-to-office requirement [12]
- the manufacturing-facilities risk factor, "health crises, including epidemics or pandemics, such as the COVID-19 pandemic" [13]
- the supplier-dependence risk factor, "health crises … such as the COVID-19 pandemic" [14]

**Progression in brief:**
- **FY2021 (Sept 26, 2021):** dedicated risk factor section "RISKS RELATED TO THE CORONAVIRUS (COVID-19) PANDEMIC," titled "The coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic had an adverse effect on our business and results of operations" [5], plus an MD&A statement that "we currently do not expect a significant impact on our results of operations in the future due to COVID-19" [2].
- **FY2022 (Sept 25, 2022):** retained as its own risk factor — "The COVID-19 pandemic, or a similar health crisis, may impact our business or results of operations in the future" [3][4] — and still discussed in MD&A (impairment judgments on non-marketable equity investments, China lockdowns) [21][22].
- **FY2023 (Sept 24, 2023):** removed as a standalone risk factor; COVID-19 survives only as an example inside broader operational risk factors [11]–[14]. MD&A no longer names it, pivoting to the Israel-Hamas war and generic pandemics [15].
- **FY2024 (Sept 29, 2024) and FY2025 (Sept 28, 2025):** the name "COVID-19" is dropped entirely, replaced by "pandemics or other health crises" [16][17][20][6][8].

So the last named appearance is the **FY2023 10-K**, and the last MD&A appearance was **FY2022** (Item 7). Note the data covers Qualcomm's last five fiscal years (FY2021–FY2025), so "last appeared" means the most recent year within that window.

question: Which of these companies name TSMC in the risk factors (Item 1A) of their most recent 10-K: AMD, Broadcom, Intel, Microchip, NVIDIA?
answer:
**Yes — AMD, Broadcom and Intel name TSMC in Item 1A of their latest 10-K. Microchip and NVIDIA do not.**

| Company (latest FY) | TSMC in Item 1A? | What they say |
|---|---|---|
| **AMD** (FY2025) | Yes | Relies on TSMC for "all wafers for microprocessor and GPU products at 7 nanometer (nm) or smaller nodes" [30]; warns that a TSMC shortfall at ≤7nm "could have a material adverse effect on our business" [31] |
| **Broadcom** (FY2025) | Yes | "During fiscal year 2025, approximately 95% of the wafers manufactured by our CMs were produced by TSMC," adding that TSMC could prioritize other customers or raise prices [34] |
| **Intel** (FY2025) | Yes | Warns its products business "would, over time, become dependent on third-party foundries, particularly TSMC… We have no long-term contract with TSMC" [39]; some advanced products are "exclusively manufactured by TSMC" [41] |
| **Microchip** (FY2026) | No | Risk factors refer only generically to "our Taiwan-based third-party wafer foundries" and to reliance on outside foundries (~65% of FY2026 net sales), without naming TSMC [14][18] |
| **NVIDIA** (FY2026) | No | Item 1A discusses foundry reliance and Taiwan/South Korea concentration but does not name TSMC [9][13]; TSMC is named in **Item 1 Business**: "We utilize foundries, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited, or TSMC, and Samsung…" [24] |

question: How did Microsoft's effective tax rate change from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026? Give each year's figure.
answer:
Microsoft’s effective tax rate rose **6.3 percentage points**, from **13.1% in fiscal 2022** to **19.4% in fiscal 2026** [9][10].

| Fiscal year (ended June 30) | Effective tax rate |
|---|---:|
| 2022 | **13.1%** [9] |
| 2023 | **19.0%** [12] |
| 2024 | **18.2%** [12] |
| 2025 | **17.6%** [12] |
| 2026 | **19.4%** [10] |

The rate jumped in 2023 largely because fiscal 2022 included a **$3.3 billion net tax benefit** from transferring intangible properties, making 2022 unusually low [2][5]. It then eased in 2024–2025 before rising in 2026, which Microsoft attributed primarily to changes in the geographic mix of earnings and tax expenses [3][4][11].

question: How did Broadcom's risk-factor statement about its largest end customers change between its fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 10-Ks?
answer:
Broadcom’s risk-factor disclosure on customer concentration shifted materially between the two filings:

- **FY2023 10-K:** Broadcom said it believed aggregate sales, through all channels, to **Apple and its top five end customers** represented approximately **20% and 35%** of net revenue, respectively [3]. It also stated separately that Apple was about **20%** and the top five were about **35%** in both FY2023 and FY2022 [9][11].
- **FY2024 10-K:** Broadcom dropped the Apple-specific statement and said aggregate sales to its **top five end customers** were approximately **40%** of net revenue in FY2024, up from **35%** in FY2023 [14][17].

So the key changes were: **top-five end-customer concentration rose from 35% to 40%**, and the **named Apple concentration disclosure was removed** in FY2024 [9][14][17].

question: What were Qualcomm's fiscal 2025 revenues and net income, and what does the filing say about future product revenue from Huawei?
answer:
**Qualcomm fiscal 2025 (year ended Sept 28, 2025)**

- **Revenues:** $44.28 billion [1] — up 14% from $39.0 billion in fiscal 2024 [5]
- **Net income:** $5.54 billion [2] — down 45% from $10.1 billion in fiscal 2024 [5]

Note: the net income decline is largely explained by a $5.7 billion charge to income tax expense in Q4 fiscal 2025 to establish a valuation allowance against federal deferred tax assets, related to the expected applicability of the CAMT under the OBBB enacted in July 2025 [6].

**Huawei: future product revenue**

The filing states that in May 2024 the U.S. Department of Commerce revoked the export license under which Qualcomm previously sold 4G and certain other integrated circuit products to Huawei, and that "**we do not expect to receive any further product revenues from Huawei**." It adds that to the extent Huawei's devices take share from OEMs that use Qualcomm products (in China or elsewhere), results of operations and cash flows could be further impacted [3].

Separately, on licensing: beginning in the second quarter of fiscal 2025, QTL revenues did not include royalties from Huawei, whose license agreement had expired [4].
